Molecular shapes: the VSEPR model

Driving question

How does a Lewis structure predict the shape of a molecule in three dimensions, and why does that shape matter?

First, we count domains and name the shapes. Then we test polarity.

Safety. No demonstration in this lesson: the balloons, carbon dioxide and water appear by picture only. If you tie real balloons for the hook, ask about latex allergies first. Data and sources. OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 7.6 Molecular Structure and Polarity. Measured geometries of every 3D model: NIST CCCBDB experimental data (CH₄ H–C–H 109.5°; NH₃ H–N–H 106.7°; H₂O H–O–H 104.5°; CH₂O H–C–H 116.1° and H–C–O 121.9°; CO₂ and HCN 180°); the limit card of slide 19 uses NIST CCCBDB H₂S 92.1° and PH₃ 93.3°. Electronegativity: the Pauling values of Lesson 4.1 (H 2.20, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44). History: Sidgwick and Powell 1940, Bakerian Lecture, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 176, 153; Gillespie and Nyholm 1957, Inorganic Stereochemistry, Quarterly Reviews 11, 339. Honors (notes only, not assessed). HCN is linear but polar: its two ends differ, and N pulls harder than H. CH₂O is trigonal planar and polar: the C=O bond is far more polar than the C–H bonds. BF₃ is trigonal planar with 120° angles and three identical B–F bonds, so their bond pulls cancel and BF₃ is nonpolar; boron has only six electrons around it. SO₂ is bent with only three domains on sulfur (two bonds and one lone pair); its O–S–O angle measures 119.5°, and both S–O bonds measure 143.2 pm, so chemists draw two resonance structures and treat the molecule as a blend of the two. Narrative thread for 4.4: the balloons. Balloons on one knot push apart; electron domains push apart the same way; the arrangement is where they settle; atoms sit at the ends of some domains and lone pairs fill the rest, so the shape is named from the atoms; wedges and dashes put the 3D shape on paper; lone pairs push harder, so angles shrink; where the bond pulls point decides polar or nonpolar; the model has limits. Driving question

How does a Lewis structure predict the shape of a molecule in three dimensions, and why does that shape matter?

Write · 60 s

  1. I think water is bent because .
Reading opener: carbon dioxide and water each have three atoms, yet CO₂ is a gas at room temperature and water is a liquid that dissolves salt and sugar. Part of the difference is shape: CO₂ is straight and water is bent. A Lewis structure shows bonds and lone pairs but not the shape; VSEPR predicts the shape from the Lewis structure.

The color code: a domain lobe is the accent color; a lone-pair lobe is the electron color (violet, yellow on the dark theme) with its two electrons, each with a minus mark; δ+ is warm and δ− is teal; nonmetal symbols are green. The atom colors of the 3D models are a separate code (CPK); their caption is on every 3D slide.

Electron domains

Rule

Count the domains on the central atom. Each bonded atom and each lone pair is one domain.

Ammonia, NH3

Nitrogen has three bonds and one lone pair.

Domains on N3 + 1 = 4

Water, H2O

Oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs.

Domains on O2 + 2 = 4

Methane, CH4

Carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs.

Domains on C4 + 0 = 4

Outer atoms

Lone pairs on the outer atoms belong to those atoms. They do not count.

Domains on C in HCN2 + 0 = 2

Check

H2O: how many domains are on oxygen?

  1. A2
  2. B4
  3. C6

B. Two bonds and two lone pairs.

Reading §4.4.1: each region of electrons around the central atom is an electron domain. A lone pair on the central atom is one domain; a bond to another atom is one domain, whether single, double or triple. Count the bonded atoms, then add the central atom’s lone pairs; lone pairs on the outer atoms belong to those atoms and do not count. Ammonia: three bonds and one lone pair, four domains. Thread: the balloons. Each domain is one balloon tied at the central atom.

Multiple bonds count once

Formaldehyde, CH2O

The C=O bond is ringed once. Two C–H bonds add two more.

Domains on C3 + 0 = 3

Carbon dioxide, CO2

Each C=O double bond counts once.

Domains on C2 + 0 = 2

Hydrogen cyanide, HCN

A single bond and a triple bond make two domains.

Domains on C2 + 0 = 2

Domains on the central atom

MoleculeBonded atomsLone pairsDomains
CO2202
HCN202
CH2O303
CH4404
NH3314
H2O224

Rule

A double or triple bond counts as one domain. All of its shared pairs point toward the same atom.

Check

CCl4: each Cl has three lone pairs. How many domains surround carbon?

  1. A4
  2. B8
  3. C16

A. Four bonds, no lone pairs on carbon.

Reading §4.4.1 Multiple bonds count once: a double bond holds two shared pairs and a triple bond three, but all of them lie between the same two atoms and point the same way from the central atom, so each counts as one domain. HCN: a single bond to H and a triple bond to N, no lone pairs on C: two domains. Misconception to listen for: a double bond is two domains. Thread: the balloons. A double or triple bond is one fat balloon, not two or three.

Domains spread apart

Rule

Domains repel, so they spread as far apart as possible. Two are linear, three are trigonal planar and four are tetrahedral.

Predict

Where do two domains go?

Two domains

They point opposite ways: linear.

Ideal angle180°

Predict

Where do three domains go?

Three domains

They make a flat triangle: trigonal planar.

Ideal angle120°

Predict

Can four domains stay flat?

Four domains

They point to the corners of a tetrahedron. They are not flat.

Ideal angle109.5°

Check

Three domains spread into…

  1. Aa line, 180°
  2. Ba flat triangle, 120°
  3. Ca tetrahedron, 109.5°

B. Three domains are farthest apart in a flat triangle.

Reading §4.4.2: every electron domain is a region of negative charge, so the domains repel. The VSEPR model (valence shell electron pair repulsion) says the domains around a central atom spread as far apart as possible; the directions they settle in are the electron-domain arrangement: two linear (180°), three trigonal planar (120°), four tetrahedral (109.5°). Thread: the balloons. Domains push apart like balloons on one knot, as far as they can.

Four domains in three dimensions

Atom colors show the element, not the charge.

Methane on paper

The flat drawing shows the bonds 90° apart.

Methane in 3D

The real molecule is not flat. Its bonds spread farther apart.

H–C–H anglemeasured 109.5°

Ideal angles

DomainsArrangementIdeal angle
2linear180°
3trigonal planar120°
4tetrahedral109.5°

Rule

In 3D, four domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron. They are 109.5° apart, not 90° as on paper.

Check

The H–C–H angle in methane is…

  1. A90°
  2. B109.5°
  3. C120°

B. Four domains in 3D: 109.5°.

Reading §4.4.2 Four domains in three dimensions: a Lewis structure is drawn on flat paper, so methane’s bonds look 90° apart. A real molecule is three-dimensional; methane’s bonds point to the four corners of a tetrahedron, a pyramid with four triangular faces, and every H–C–H angle is 109.5°. The angle between two bonds on one atom is a bond angle; each arrangement has its own ideal angle. Thread: the balloons. Four balloons cannot stay flat; one points at you.

Lone pairs and molecular shape

Atom colors show the element, not the charge.

Rule

The arrangement counts every domain. The molecular geometry is named from the atoms only. Lone pairs are not atoms.

No lone pairs

Four bonds: the shape is tetrahedral, like the arrangement.

Predict

One bond becomes a lone pair. What shape is left?

One lone pair

An atom leaves, but its domain stays. Three atoms make a pyramid: trigonal pyramidal.

Two lone pairs

Two atoms leave. The three atoms left make a bent shape.

Ammonia in 3D

The lone pair takes the space above nitrogen.

Water in 3D

Two lone pairs take the space above oxygen.

Check

Water: four domains, two lone pairs. Its shape is…

  1. Atetrahedral
  2. Btrigonal pyramidal
  3. Cbent

C. Three atoms, not in a line: bent.

Reading §4.4.3: the molecular geometry is named from the positions of the atoms only. Lone pairs take up room but are not atoms, so the name leaves them out. With no lone pairs the geometry matches the arrangement; with lone pairs the two names differ. Methane, ammonia and water all have four domains in a tetrahedral arrangement: methane tetrahedral, ammonia trigonal pyramidal (three H below N), water bent. Misconception to listen for: the arrangement is the shape. Thread: the balloons. A lone pair is a balloon with no atom at its end, so the shape is named from the atoms.

Wedges and dashes

Rule

Line: in the page. Solid wedge: toward you. Dashed wedge: away from you.

Methane

Two lines, one solid wedge and one dashed wedge.

Ammonia

One of each kind. The lone pair sits on top.

Flat molecules

CO2 and CH2O are flat. They need only lines.

Check

A dashed wedge shows a bond that points…

  1. Atoward you
  2. Baway from you
  3. Cin the page

B. Dashes go behind the page.

Reading §4.4.4: a wedge-and-dash drawing shows a 3D shape on flat paper. A plain line is a bond in the page; a solid wedge points out of the page, toward you; a dashed wedge points behind the page, away from you. Linear and trigonal planar molecules are flat, so lines are enough. Methane needs all three kinds; ammonia uses one of each, with its lone pair on top. Thread: the balloons. Wedges and dashes put the 3D directions of the balloons on flat paper.

Measured bond angles

Atom colors show the element, not the charge.

Ideal and measured (NIST CCCBDB)

MoleculeLone pairsIdealMeasured
CH40109.5°109.5°
NH31109.5°106.7°
H2O2109.5°104.5°
CH2O0120°116.1° (H–C–H), 121.9° (H–C–O)
CO20180°180°

Rule

Lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs. So they make bond angles smaller than the ideal.

Formaldehyde

In CH2O, the double bond takes more room than the single bonds.

Check

Which molecule has the smallest bond angle?

  1. ACH4
  2. BNH3
  3. CH2O

C. Two lone pairs push the bonds closest: 104.5°.

Reading §4.4.4 Measured bond angles: the ideal angles come from the model; chemists measure real angles, and the NIST CCCBDB collects them. The model statement: a lone pair takes up more room than a bonding pair, so each lone pair pushes the bonds a little closer: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 106.7°, H₂O 104.5°. In CH₂O the double bond takes more room than the single bonds: H–C–H 116.1°, H–C–O 121.9°. Thread: the balloons. A lone-pair balloon is fatter, so it pushes the bonds closer together.

Polar molecules

Rule

Polar bonds pull toward the δ− atom. In a straight or evenly spread shape, equal bond pulls cancel. The molecule is nonpolar. In a bent or pyramidal shape, bond pulls add up. The molecule is polar.

Carbon dioxide

Each C=O bond pulls toward O, the δ− atom. The arrow shows that pull.

Predict

Do the two bond pulls cancel or add up?

Straight

The two bond pulls are equal and opposite. They cancel, so CO₂ is nonpolar.

Water

Each O–H bond pulls toward O. But water is bent.

Predict

Do the two bond pulls cancel or add up?

Bent

Both bond pulls point partly toward O. They add up, so water is polar.

Check

CO2 has two polar bonds. Why is the molecule nonpolar?

  1. Athe bonds are not polar
  2. Bthe two bond pulls cancel in a straight line
  3. Coxygen does not pull electrons

B. Equal, opposite bond pulls cancel.

Reading §4.4.5: a bond between atoms with different electronegativity is polar; the atom that pulls harder carries δ−. Whether a whole molecule is polar depends on its polar bonds and its shape. CO₂: each C=O is polar (difference 0.89), but the molecule is linear, so the equal bond pulls cancel: nonpolar. H₂O: each O–H is polar (1.24) and the molecule is bent, so the bond pulls add up toward O: polar. Misconception to listen for: polar bonds guarantee a polar molecule. Thread: the balloons. Where the bond pulls point decides polar or nonpolar.

Word bank: polar bent add up cancel

Sample answer

The O–H bonds are polar. Water is bent. The bond pulls add up, so water is polar.

Reading §4.4.5: ammonia is polar for the same reason as water: its three N–H bond pulls (difference 0.84) all point partly toward nitrogen. Methane is nonpolar: each C–H bond has a difference of only 0.35, and the four bonds point evenly in all directions. The same three questions every time: are the bonds polar, what is the shape, do the bond pulls cancel. Thread: the balloons. The same three questions every time: polar bonds, shape, do the bond pulls cancel.

A model with limits

What it does

VSEPR predicts the five shapes. It explains why lone pairs make angles smaller.

Exact angles

It does not give exact angles. Those come from measurements.

Moving electrons

It does not show how electrons move.

Limit of the model

H2S has four domains, like water. Its angle measures 92.1°. PH3 measures 93.3°. The simple model does not fit them.

Measured angleH₂S 92.1°PH₃ 93.3°

Rule

VSEPR is a model. It predicts the five shapes well, but not every exact angle. It does not show electrons moving.

Reading §4.4.5 A model with limits: in 1940 Nevil Sidgwick and Herbert Powell proposed, in a Bakerian Lecture to the Royal Society, that a molecule’s shape follows from the electron pairs around its central atom; in 1957 Ronald Gillespie and Ronald Nyholm turned the idea into detailed rules, the VSEPR model. The model predicts all five shapes and explains why lone pairs shrink angles, but it does not give exact angles and does not show how electrons move. Limit box (text only): H₂S 92.1° and PH₃ 93.3° (NIST CCCBDB), far below the slightly-under-109.5° VSEPR predicts. Thread: the balloons are a model, and every model has limits.
